Letting the model write and run R code is the most flexible tool you can give
an agent, and the most dangerous. Deputy offers three ways to do it, which
differ in two respects: whether R state survives between calls, and whether
the code is confined by an OS sandbox.

| Option | State between calls | Confinement |
|---|---|---|
| `tool_run_r_code` | none; each call starts a new R process | your user account's access |
| `RSession` | variables, packages and plots persist | your user account's access |
| MCP Console, through `mcp_console_connection()` | persists; R, Python and SQL share data | OS sandbox |

Deputy calls the first two *trusted-code tools*. A separate process protects
your R session from crashes and runaway loops, but the code can still read,
write and send anything your account can. Use them when you trust the model,
the prompt and every input the agent reads, for example your own analysis on
your own data. Otherwise use a sandbox.

The trusted-code tools don't pass on your environment variables, and R
there doesn't read `.Renviron`. The code sees the variables that locate
programs, libraries, locales and temporary files, such as `PATH`, `HOME`,
`LANG` and `TMPDIR`, but API keys in your environment aren't handed to it.
Name any others it needs with `env`, for example
`RSession$new(agent, env = c("HTTPS_PROXY", "NO_PROXY"))`,
`tools_code(env = "HTTPS_PROXY")` or `tools_preset("dev", env = ...)`. Proxy
settings match in either case. `env = "inherit"` passes everything, keys
included.

This keeps keys out of what the code is given, not out of its reach. Code
running as your account can still read your R session's starting environment
through the operating system, and any file your account can read,
`.Renviron` included. The site `Renviron.site` still applies, and so does a
project `.Rprofile` for `tool_run_r_code`. To keep keys from the code, run
the agent under an account that can't read them, or use a sandbox.

## One-off R code

`tool_run_r_code` runs each snippet in a fresh R process started with callr,
with a 30-second timeout, and returns the printed output and result. Enable
it with `r_code = TRUE`:

```{r}
library(deputy)

agent <- Agent$new(
  chat = ellmer::chat("openai/gpt-6.2-sol"),
  tools = c(tools_data(), list(tool_run_r_code)),
  permissions = Permissions(r_code = TRUE, file_write = FALSE)
)
agent$run_sync("How many rows of mtcars have more than 4 cylinders?")
```

`tool_run_bash` does the same for shell commands and needs `bash = TRUE`.
Nothing carries over between calls, so the model has to reload data each time.

## A persistent R session

`RSession` gives one agent its own R worker process. Variables and loaded
packages persist between calls, so the model can load data once and work with
it over many steps. Plots come back to the model as images.

```{r}
agent <- Agent$new(
  chat = ellmer::chat("openai/gpt-6.2-sol"),
  permissions = Permissions(r_code = TRUE, file_write = FALSE)
)
worker <- RSession$new(agent)
agent$register_tools(worker$tools())

agent$run_sync("Load mtcars, fit mpg ~ wt, and plot the residuals.")
agent$run_sync("Now add hp to the model. Did the fit improve?")

worker$close()
```

The worker starts on the first call. Calls run one at a time in order, each
with a 30-second timeout by default, and each starts in the agent's working
directory. `$cancel()`, or a timeout, stops the worker and discards its
variables; the next call starts a fresh worker and says so. Call `$close()`
when the conversation ends, for example from `session$onSessionEnded()` in
Shiny.

A saved conversation keeps the code, output and plots. Use an explicit
checkpoint to keep selected worker variables across a restart.

The worker loads packages from your session's `.libPaths()`. To give it a
library of its own, for example one the model installs packages into, name
the directories in order with `libpath`:
`RSession$new(agent, libpath = c(my_lib, .libPaths()))`. Your own session's
search path doesn't change.

Static plots from base graphics, ggplot2, grid and patchwork are captured.
To keep supported interactive outputs, opt into an artifact directory.

### Reopen interactive R results

Use an existing private directory and a stable host owner ID. Visible Plotly,
DT and Leaflet widgets with bundled resources, and tables from gt or flextable,
can be exported to HTML. htmlwidgets export uses Pandoc. The result includes a
bounded text summary and a static PNG when the renderer can capture one.
Browser previews use optional webshot2 and Chrome. Flextable exports its own
static image. The HTML, text and image share the call's output budget.

```{r}
worker <- RSession$new(
  agent,
  artifact_dir = app_artifact_dir,
  artifact_owner_id = app_owner_id
)
agent$register_tools(worker$tools())

# In a host callback, use the saved ContentToolResult for this conversation.
interactive <- Filter(
  function(segment) !is.null(segment$artifact$id),
  result@extra$deputy_r$segments
)
if (length(interactive)) {
  frame <- worker$artifact_frame(interactive[[1L]]$artifact$id)
  # Return the frame from shiny::renderUI() for this authorized conversation.
}
```

After a restart, load the saved conversation and recreate `RSession` with
the original owner, Agent and session IDs and artifact directory. The saved
tool card carries the display evidence and reference. The host can show the
verified frame beside that card without starting an R worker. The frame
isolates the document from the host page and restricts subresource loads to
bundled content. Use local layers for Leaflet maps. Server-backed outputs
require a live renderer. The host controls authorization and retention.

### Recover selected R data after a restart

Give each conversation a stable owner, Agent and session ID from your
application. Configure an existing private directory where your application
keeps checkpoint artifacts. The example uses a temporary directory. For
reopening after a supervisor restart, use durable storage and retain the
checkpoint receipt's ID in your application.

```{r}
directory <- tempfile()
dir.create(directory, mode = "0700")

open_worker <- function() {
  agent <- Agent$new(
    chat = ellmer::chat("openai/gpt-6.2-sol"),
    agent_id = "analysis",
    session_id = "analysis-17"
  )
  RSession$new(
    agent,
    checkpoint_dir = directory,
    checkpoint_owner_id = "research-team"
  )
}

worker <- open_worker()
promises::then(worker$run("measurements <- mtcars[1:5, ]; scratch <- 10"), function(result) {
  worker$checkpoint("measurements")
}) |>
  promises::then(function(receipt) {
    worker$close()
    reopened <- open_worker()
    promises::then(reopened$restore_checkpoint(receipt$id), function(restored) {
      print(restored$bindings)
      reopened$run("nrow(measurements)")
    }) |>
      promises::finally(function() reopened$close())
  })
```

Checkpoint operations and R executions share one queue. Wait for the restore
promise to resolve before submitting dependent code. Captures support ordinary
R data such as base data frames, matrices, factors and lists of vectors. The
artifact stores at most 8 MiB of serialized data. A receipt identifies the
selected bindings and their capture generation. The restore receipt adds the
generation that imported them. Variables outside the selection must be
recreated. Configure the new Agent and register its tools as you would for a
new worker.

Keep R data checkpoints, conversation output and job or approval effect records
in their respective stores. Importing data does not repeat the R expressions
that produced it. A failed expression can leave partial changes in R or in
files and services. If a job's effect outcome is indeterminate, inspect its
external receipt before deciding whether to make another request.

### Call your tools from R code

An R session can let the model's code call some of the agent's other tools, so
it can fetch data with a tool and then analyse the result in R:

```{r}
worker <- RSession$new(agent, tools = "fetch_measurements")
agent$register_tools(worker$tools())
```

Inside the session, the code calls `tools$fetch_measurements(...)` and gets
the tool's return value as an ordinary R object. Each of these calls goes
through the agent's permissions, hooks and usage limits like any other tool
call. The selected tools must be registered with `convert = FALSE` and check
their own arguments, and they can't pause for a durable approval.

## Sandboxed R, Python and SQL with MCP Console

[MCP Console](https://github.com/posit-dev/mcp-console) is an OS-sandboxed
workbench. Its single `send` tool runs R, Python and DuckDB SQL cells in one
worker, so a data frame made in R can be queried in SQL and read from Python in
the same conversation, with optional named sessions (`session`) and journal
notes (`note`).

```{r}
agent <- Agent$new(
  chat = ellmer::chat("openai/gpt-6.2-sol"),
  permissions = Permissions(bash = TRUE, web = TRUE)
)
console <- mcp_console_connection(
  agent,
  command = Sys.getenv("DEPUTY_MCP_CONSOLE_BIN"),
  dependencies = "allow"
)
agent$register_tools(console$tools())
# ...
console$close()
```

Install MCP Console 0.4.0 yourself (for example with
`uv tool install mcp-console==0.4.0`) and pass the path to the executable.
Deputy checks the version before starting it, and works with mcptools 1.0.2
and 1.0.3.

In its sandbox, code can read files but can't reach the network, and it can
write only to private temporary storage and to paths you allow. Deputy keeps it
that way: it refuses options that would turn the sandbox off, widen file
access, add a proxy, override `tool.description`, or run code somewhere else.
It accepts `--writable-root PATH` and safe `-c` overrides including
`-c sandbox.profile=workspace` (write in the agent's working directory),
`-c sandbox.profile=read_only`, `-c sandbox.network=restricted`,
`-c r.resolution=disabled|fixed|explicit`,
`-c python.resolution=fixed|explicit`,
`-c tool.parameters.requirements.enabled=false`, and `-c sessions.max=N`. A
project config file, `.agents/console/config.yaml`, can change the sandbox
policy, so Deputy refuses to start when one exists and passes
`--no-project-config` unless you have reviewed it and pass
`project_config = TRUE`. After starting, Deputy checks the sandbox the server
reports and disconnects unless it is the native sandbox with restricted
networking.

`send` runs code, so Deputy treats it like a shell command: the agent needs
`bash = TRUE`, plus `web = TRUE` because the server doesn't annotate its tools.
Read-only and plan modes deny it.

MCP Console can also install the packages that code asks for using its separate
resolver sandbox (which has network access to package repositories and cache
writes). It does this when a call lists `requirements`, and by default R also
resolves missing packages automatically on `library()` or `::`. With the
default `dependencies = "deny"`, Deputy refuses to connect while `requirements`
is exposed; either pass `dependencies = "allow"` or disable preparation
explicitly (for example with `-c r.resolution=disabled`,
`-c python.resolution=fixed`, and
`-c tool.parameters.requirements.enabled=false`). With
`dependencies = "allow"`, a call that lists `requirements` also needs
`install_packages = TRUE` in the agent's permissions. Set variables such as
`UV_CACHE_DIR` or `MCP_CONSOLE_HOME` through `env` to control cache and
recording locations.

Calls wait up to 2.5 seconds. Longer work keeps running and returns
`[running; poll with an empty send]`, and the model collects the output with an
empty `send`. `mcp_console_control(console, "interrupt")` interrupts a cell and
keeps the session's state; `mcp_console_control(console, "restart")` discards
all R, Python and SQL state (pass `session = "name"` to target a named
session). If the restarted worker isn't ready within 2.5 seconds, Deputy closes
the connection and you need to start a new one.

MCP Console records every call, note, output and plot under
`.agents/console/sessions/` when `.agents/console` already exists in the
agent's working directory, or otherwise under `$MCP_CONSOLE_HOME/sessions/`
(`~/.agents/console/sessions/` by default). Recordings aren't redacted and
aren't deleted automatically; `console$status()$execution$recordings` gives the
path.
